items.title: Jimmy Heath — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: We were doing okay with the Heath Brothers as the three of us.

ctx.x: When we did, I think we had been together and made records for Columbia, and CBS, and that was a time earlier. But then we did record twice, and that was in ’97 and a record called, “As We Used To Do” Still, we got dumped by Columbia and then we got to record for Concord. Then we did another on ’98 called, “jazz Family” And we proceeded to tour and play together, and go to Japan, Europe, whatever, and play in the states. We were doing okay with the Heath Brothers as the three of us. Then in 2004 we were playing…

items.title: Percy Heath — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: We were sleeping around up there, me and Jimmy. Jimmy was in that sextet, too.

ctx.x: Up in Harlem, 115th in East Harlem. We were sleeping around up there, me and Jimmy. Jimmy was in that sextet, too. But the big band made those few appearances in the theatre with that show, it was fantastic.
So you played in the sextet and in the big band? Howard McGhee’s Big Band?

items.title: Jimmy Heath interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, September 8, 2014
items.q: Percy could play a blues after leaving the MJQ [Modern Jazz Quartet] and playing with the Heath brothers

ctx.x: Well I consider Cannonball Adderley as a country preacher in his deliverance of his melodic performances. You know he had the south in his playing as well as the science. And people who have that, they’ve got the whole thing as far as I’m concerned. Coltrane

had it. My brother Percy had it. He was born in North Carolina and I was born in Philadelphia. And Percy could play a blues after leaving the MJQ [Modern Jazz Quartet] and playing with the Heath brothers he started to play what I call the baby bass, which was something that Ray Brown created. It was a cello body strung up like a bass. And Percy could play the blues and get it over every time. Because he was born in North Carolina in the south. There’s something about being born in the south that, at that time, of…
You said something, just in what you said about the blues makes me wonder — you were talking about how jazz is sometimes now thought of as the “white man’s music.” And what is the reason for that?
